# Malakut — Searching for Malakut

**This is an AI-assisted philosophical investigation. This text was generated by AI (model: GPT-6) from Babak Mahmoudi's stated questions and direction, with source research by the AI. Revised on 27 November 2026 to reflect his affirmed working distinctions; the wording below awaits his review. AI-generated prose must not be mistaken for his own writing or for established philosophical conclusions.**

## Three domains of discourse

Malakut begins by distinguishing three useful domains of discourse:

| Domain | Working meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Physical World** | Physical things, events, processes, and relations. |
| **Human Experience** | The lived experience of perceiving, feeling, thinking, and being conscious. |
| **Descriptions** | Shareable thought contents, understood broadly in the spirit of Popper's World 3, including scientific theories, mathematical formulations, stories, and other intellectual or cultural contents. |

The division is a convenience for articulating questions and organizing inquiry. It does not itself assert three separate metaphysical entities, independently existing worlds, or fundamentally different ways of being. “Realms,” when used, is a provisional and evocative expression for these domains. Their boundaries, overlap, and usefulness remain open to revision.

The methodological preference is Carnapian: clarify the framework in which an existence claim is made and assess the usefulness of adopting it. Deeper ontology is deferred for investigation. Questions of dependence, emergence, and fundamentality remain central; no commitment is inferred merely from introducing a category of discourse. [Source: Carnap, §2](https://ditext.com/carnap/carnap.html).

“Descriptions” is a deliberately broad project term, extending beyond description in ordinary usage. It names objective thought contents in the spirit of Popper's broader cultural scope. Here, “objective” distinguishes a content that can be shared, interpreted, and criticized from a particular person's experience of thinking it; it does not mean that the content is true. A physical inscription, an experience of understanding it, and its content must be distinguished, without deciding in advance how they depend on one another.

This adoption concerns scope and vocabulary. It does not adopt Popper's realism about World 3 as an established conclusion. The [dialogue on frameworks and Descriptions](Dialogs/2026-11-27-frameworks-and-descriptions.md) records the development of these distinctions.

No claim of originality is made for the threefold proposal. Its intellectual ancestry remains a subject of inquiry.

## The relationships are the central question

The project is especially concerned with how these domains relate, including their possible dependence and fundamentality.

**Physical World and Human Experience.** What does it mean to say that experience emerges from the physical world? Does “emergence” explain anything, or name a relationship still needing explanation? What would establish that an account of physical processes accounts for lived experience?

**Human Experience and Descriptions.** How does experience become articulated in language, concepts, mathematics, or theories? What is the difference between an experience, the act of describing it, and the content of that description? Can descriptions in turn shape how we experience?

**Descriptions and Physical World.** How do descriptions refer to physical things and succeed in predicting their behavior? In particular, what is being claimed when natural laws are said to govern the physical world? If a law is expressed in a description, does the description control events, represent an independently existing constraint, or summarize a pattern? These possibilities must be distinguished and argued for.

A theory guiding an engineer's actions and a law allegedly governing nature raise different questions about influence. Explaining the first does not by itself explain the second.

These are questions for investigation. Neither the emergence of experience nor the governing power of natural laws is assumed to have been established.

## Nearby proposals and the question of credit

Roger Penrose is the comparison that prompted this inquiry. In *The Road to Reality*, §1.4, he distinguishes physical, mental, and Platonic mathematical worlds, emphasizing the puzzling connections among them. His mathematical world should not simply be identified with “Descriptions”: mathematical formulations fall within the present working category, while the status of mathematical objects and structures, and their relation to those formulations, remains open. [Source: Penrose, chapter 1](https://astroweb.iag.usp.br/~amancio/mpa5003_notas/road-to-reality-roger-penrose.pdf).

Karl Popper supplies another close precedent. In his lecture *Three Worlds*, he distinguishes the physical world, subjective experience, and the products of the human mind, including languages and scientific theories. The present project adopts “Descriptions” as its working name for objective thought contents, with the broader scope that makes Popper's proposal more suitable here than an exclusively mathematical third world. This alignment leaves Popper's ontological arguments open to examination and does not settle historical priority. [Source: Popper, *Three Worlds*](https://tannerlectures.org/documents/three-worlds/).

The historical inquiry should establish what each author claimed and where the present proposal agrees or differs. Similar terminology alone does not establish identical views.

## Why “Malakut”?

The project's name comes from the line:

> مرغ باغ ملکوتم، نیم از عالم خاک

*“I am a bird of the garden of Malakut; I am not of the world of dust.”*  
— AI translation of the Persian line.

The line gives the investigation its motivating image: a search for this **Malakut**. What might it mean to speak of belonging to a realm other than the physical world? How does that poetic expression bear on experience, descriptions, and their relation to physical existence?

The search begins with the image and the questions it opens. Whether it points toward a distinct realm, an aspect of experience, or another interpretation remains to be explored.

**Attribution:** The fuller poem beginning «روزها فکر من این است و همه شب سخنم» is commonly attributed to Rumi (Jalal al-Din Muhammad Balkhi), but its attribution is disputed. The quoted Malakut line also appears in Homam Tabrizi's ghazal 142. The authorship of the fuller poem and the transmission of this individual verse are distinct questions; neither a reference to Shams Tabrizi within a version of the poem nor its popular attribution settles them. A critical edition must be checked before asserting its status within the *Divan-e Shams*, and the direction of any borrowing remains unestablished here. [Homam text](https://ganjoor.net/homam/ghazalho/sh142/) · [Discussion of the disputed Rumi attribution, by Latif Nazemi](https://maulana-haus.de/خاستگاه-شعراز-دیدگاه-مولانا/).
